title: The Church of the East
hookLine: Christians who traveled the Silk Road to China and India in the first millennium

lines: A CROSS RISING FROM A LOTUS.
cards: In the 1620s, workers digging near Xi'an, in China, pulled a huge stone slab out of the ground. Taller than a man, with a cross carved at the top, rising out of a lotus flower.
Below it, nearly two thousand Chinese characters, and a border of writing in Syriac. The stone had been set up in 781.

It told how a monk named Alopen reached the Tang emperor's capital in 635, carrying scriptures, and how the emperor welcomed him, had the books translated, and let him build a monastery. Christians in China, in the 600s.

teach.h: A CHURCH BEYOND ROME, IN PERSIA.
teach.b: The Church of the East grew up in Persia, beyond the Roman Empire's eastern border, among Christians who prayed in Syriac, a cousin of Jesus's own Aramaic.
Its leader, the catholicos, sat in Seleucia-Ctesiphon, near modern Baghdad. Outside Rome, it went its own way on the councils.
Westerners long called it Nestorian, after a bishop condemned in 431, a label the church didn't choose and many today find misleading.

teach.h: ALONG THE SILK ROAD TO CHINA.
teach.b: Along the Silk Road, with its caravans, oases and monasteries, merchants and monks from this church carried the gospel across Central Asia to China, and down to India, where the Saint Thomas Christians trace their faith to the apostle Thomas himself.
In China they called their faith the luminous teaching. At its height, around 1300, this one church stretched from the Mediterranean to the Pacific, with more territory than any church in Europe.

A monk from near Beijing, Rabban Sauma, traveled west and met the king of France in 1287, and the pope in 1288. Then came centuries of hardship: plagues, conquests, the collapse of the Mongol empire, massacres.
The church shrank almost to nothing in China and Central Asia.

teach.h: SMALL NOW, MANY OF THEM REFUGEES.
teach.b: Its heirs today, the Assyrian Church of the East, the Ancient Church of the East, and churches in communion with Rome such as the Chaldeans, are small, many of them refugees from Iraq and Syria.

teach.h: UNTO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.
teach.b: In Acts, Jesus told his friends they would be his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth." Most maps of Christian history draw that line going west. This church went east too, early and far.

how: The Assyrian Church of the East and its sister churches still pray in Syriac, keep an ancient liturgy called the Liturgy of Addai and Mari, and honor the cross without a figure on it.

games.q: it's 635. a foreign monk arrives at the Tang emperor's capital with books nobody there can read. you're the emperor. what do you do?
o: have the books translated and let him build a monastery.
make his faith the law of the land.
games.why: the Xi'an stone says the emperor welcomed Alopen, had the scriptures translated, and allowed a monastery to be built.

practice: On a map of Asia, trace a finger from Baghdad east, across Iran and the mountains of Central Asia, to Xi'an; then back, and down to Kerala, on India's southwest coast.

Thousands of miles, walked by monks and merchants more than a thousand years ago. If you pray, pray for the Christians who still live along that road, and those who had to leave it; if not, let the size of the map sink in.
